sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern will persist into the end of week as a series of disturbances moves through the area. This, coupled with high astronomical tides, will continue the threat for coastal flooding through the end of the week. Unsettled conditions are expected to persist into early next week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday)
paragraphs: A frontal boundary is gradually pushing onshore into Western Washington this morning as the next system is already quickly approaching offshore. The overall forecast picture hasn't changed much with rain and wind picking up along the coast by early evening as a warm front lifts northward across the area. Rain will increase across the interior overnight with windy conditions developing across the North Interior, San Juans, and Admiralty Inlet area as well. Strongest winds will be focused along the coast and across the North Interior with some gusts in the 50 to 55 mph range, but Puget Sound will become windy as well with some gusts around 40 mph as the warm front shifts inland early Thanksgiving morning. Storm total rainfall with this next system remains in the same ballpark as previous estimates with up to 2 inches for coastal areas, 2 to 4 inches in the Olympics, 2 to 3 inches in the Cascades, and around a inch for the interior lowlands outside of the Olympic rain shadow. The trailing cold front will sweep inland Thursday afternoon with post-frontal showers, perhaps an isolated thunderstorm, and winds gradually easing.

Another, weaker system is slated to arrive later in the day on Friday as it rides over the top of an upper ridge building into California. As has been the case in recent days, coastal flooding will continue to be the headline-making hazard as some of the years highest astronomical tides combine with storm surge and high surf to produce some significant tidal anomalies and impacts to coastal communities.

sections.title: Long term (Friday night through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Ensembles are advertising a brief break with some weak upper ridging over the weekend, but, even so, it would be tough to completely remove any chance of precip for more than about 12 hours. Broad upper troughing returns to the offshore waters by early next week with another parade of systems marching onshore into the West Coast.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Southwesterly flow aloft as showers continue over western Washington this morning. Conditions mostly VFR at all terminals early this morning, the exception being HQM, where MVFR conditions are being observed in rain. Generally, expect periods of rain throughout the day today with most terminals remaining VFR. Could see a brief drop to MVFR/IFR in areas of heavier showers, but with gusty winds today, ceilings should stay VFR. The next front will arrive late this evening, with strong winds. Winds will start to pick up after 22z-03z, with gusts starting along the coast around 40 to 50 kts. Terminals in the interior will see gusts up to 35, even 40 kts through the overnight hours. Ceilings will bounce to VFR/MVFR, with lowered conditions in showers, although gusty S/SE winds should kept most terminals at VFR.

KSEA...VFR conditions continuing at the terminal throughout this afternoon with on and off showers. A front will move through late this evening into Thursday, with strong winds and more rain. S/SE winds will start to increase around 00z-03z, with sustained winds 15 to 20 kts, with gusts potentially around 30 to 35 kts at times, lasting throughout the overnight and into early morning hours on Thursday. Ceilings will likely fall to MVFR at times through the late evening, especially in heavier batches of rain. Winds will continue to remain gusty through Thursday morning.
Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system remains offshore, and will continue to bring strong winds and elevated seas to the waters today. A Storm Warning remains in effect for all coastal water zones today as a front moves in late tonight into Thursday morning. Gale Warnings also remain in effect for the East and West Entrance Strait of Juan De Fuca, and the Northern Inland Waters. Elsewhere, Small Craft Advisories will remain. Winds will stay gusty tonight into Thursday morning for most waters, with a notable difference in wind strength Thursday afternoon, where additional headlines may be needed for the transition. Additionally, there is a chance of an isolated thunderstorm or two Thursday afternoon, mainly over the coastal waters.
An surface high pressure looks to develop over the region on Friday, which would provide a brief break from winds and seas. Additional systems over the weekend may drive winds and seas up again.

Coastal seas generally 15 to 20 feet this morning will continue to stay in this range throughout the remainder of the day. Seas will start subsiding late Thursday into Friday to 10 to 15 feet. Seas will lower even further by late Friday into Saturday, where we could see seas get below 10 feet through the weekend.
Mazurkiewicz

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active weather pattern continues through the workweek with a potent atmospheric river expected Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, and potentially continuing through Friday. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding. A brief break is favored for Saturday, but active weather returns late weekend into early next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active weather pattern continues through the workweek with a potent atmospheric river expected Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, and potentially continuing through Friday. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern as strong winds offshore and rough seas coincide with monthly King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding. A brief break is favored for Saturday, but active weather returns late weekend into early next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Tuesday...Active weather remains on the menu for the Thanksgiving holiday and through the end of the workweek. An initial frontal system which brought rain showers Tuesday has pushed east of the Cascades early this morning, but another, more potent system will approach the coast later today. In the near term, the offshore-oriented pressure gradient continues to rapidly weaken behind the frontal passage, which will see east winds through terrain gaps ease today. Ahead of the next weather system, scattered rain showers may continue on the north Oregon coast and across southwestern Washington, while increasing southerly winds push temperatures about 10 degrees above normal across the region. A warm frontal passage this afternoon may bring an increase of rain shower coverage through the evening commute, but the bulk of the rain will hold off until tonight.

There is high confidence that a strong atmospheric river will affect the region tonight through Thanksgiving Day. Short-range ensemble consensus is high of IVT between 750-1000 kg/ms, supporting robust moisture transport from the south-southwest. Typical cold frontal dynamics in conjunction with orographic enhancement will yield high rainfall rates, especially tonight through Thursday morning. There is weaker consensus on Friday, with most members bringing an upper shortwave into the Pacific Northwest on the heels of the exiting AR, which despite uncertainty in its strength, should still contribute to another round of rain. Median 48-hour rainfall totals from this evening through Friday evening are 2-2.5" along the I-5 corridor, and 2.5-4" along the coast and in areas of terrain. Reasonable worst-case rainfall amounts (10% chance of occurrence) are 2.5-3.5" along I-5 and 3.5-5" along the coast and in terrain. Rainfall rates are most likely to peak early Thursday morning along the north Oregon and south Washington coasts, through the remainder of Thursday morning elsewhere along the central Oregon coast and inland to the north of Eugene, and Thursday afternoon across inland Lane County and the Cascades south of Santiam Pass. These rainfall rates may be sufficient to support nuisance flooding of urban, low-lying, or other poor drainage areas. Thanksgiving Day travelers should prepare for wet roads and possibly areas of standing water where storm drains are clogged or in typical low spots. Rainfall amounts are unlikely to support any widespread river flooding. Snow levels at or above 6-8 kft will keep the Cascades passes free of snow.

The approaching frontal system will also bring a period of gusty south winds to the region. Concerns for strong winds are the highest at the coast, where favored terrain dynamics may support the development of a coastal jet which could locally enhance wind speeds at beaches and headlands. Gusts are expected to peak between 10 PM this evening and 7 AM Thursday at 40-50 mph, but with 10-25% chances of instead peaking at 50-60 mph at any point within that period. A High Wind Watch remains in effect for the Tillamook, Clatsop, and Pacific County coasts, and residents should consider preparing for power outages on Thursday. If confidence in the occurrence of peak winds near 60 mph increases, the Watch may be upgraded to a High Wind Warning, while its cancellation should instead signal that confidence has increased in peak winds of 40-50 mph. Elsewhere across inland areas, breezy winds should be expected on Thursday, but widespread impacts are not anticipated.

There remains higher uncertainty in the potential for a trailing area of low pressure to approach the northern or central Oregon coast on Friday. If this occurs and if the low is deep enough, it could support another period of strong winds out of the south. About 20% of mid-range ensemble members depict peak wind gusts above 50 mph along the coast Friday afternoon or evening, and about 10% of members maintain strong gusts inland into the Willamette Valley. Expect this forecast to remain uncertain and very sensitive to the intensity and position of the offshore surface low which will be difficult for numerical guidance to capture given its development over the sparsely observed Northeast Pacific.

Long-range model consensus increases this weekend in transient upper-level ridging which will favor a brief dry break on Saturday. The progressive pattern then favors a return to wetter and more active weather from Sunday into early next week. -36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12z Thursday...Largely VFR conditions in place as scattered light rain showers continue to stream from southwest to northeast across the airspace, with highest coverage over the far north OR and south WA coasts including near KAST. Showers are expected to decrease in coverage through the early afternoon, then increase ahead of an approaching cold front with widespread rain favored after 03z Thu. Chances for MVFR cigs are highest at coastal terminals early this morning and after steady rain begins this afternoon, with VFR condition otherwise favored. Inland cigs are more likely to persist at 5-7 kft or higher.

Winds remain the focus through the period, with south to southeast flow continuing early this morning. Along the Willamette Valley, south winds will rise to around 10 kt with gusts increasing to 20 kt as the front approaches this evening. In the Portland area, southeast winds at 10-15 kt with gusts as high as 20-30 kt, strongest near the western entrance of the Columbia River Gorge, will begin to shift more out of the south as the front nears after 03z Thu. Along the coast, south winds around 15 kt with gusts near 25 kt this morning will increase to 20-25 kt as high as 30-40 kt this afternoon and evening.

Increasing winds at 2 kft above the surface will see periods of low-level wind shear at most terminals, highest as the frontal boundary passes overhead. Coastal terminals will see this peak speed-shear with 60-70 kt winds at 2 kft late in the period, while Portland-area terminals see more directional shear given southeast winds at the surface and 30-40 kt winds at 2 kft despite peak winds aloft occurring beyond the end of the TAF period.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions are expected through the period with isolated light rain showers this morning giving way to widespread rain by this afternoon/evening. Southeast winds continue ahead of an approaching frontal boundary, shifting more out of the south as rain begins. Low-level wind shear will remain a persistent concern as winds at 2 kft increase out of the south- southwest to 30-40 kt after 03z Thu. -36

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Multiple frontal systems will keep hazardous marine conditions in place for the next few days. While seas remain elevated behind the recent frontal passage, the morning hours today will provide a relative lull between weather systems. Hazardous Seas Warnings remain in effect until 1 PM this afternoon for seas of 15-20 ft at 13-15 seconds with a dominant southwest swell.

Another more robust frontal system arrives this afternoon into Thanksgiving Day, ushering in an additional round of hazardous winds and elevated seas. Widespread gale-force gusts are expected across the waters, with Gale Warnings in effect for most of the coastal waters including the Columbia River Bar from 1 PM this afternoon through 10 AM Thursday. The south-southwest wind direction will also support the development of a coastal jet along the north Oregon and south Washington coasts, resulting in locally higher winds within 10 NM of the coast from Cape Foulweather north to Cape Shoalwater, where a Storm Warning has been issued instead. Both wind-driven seas and the southwest swell will begin to ease by Thursday afternoon, although another period of Hazardous Seas Warnings may be needed before combined seas fall below 15 ft Friday morning. There is also a 20% chance that another area of surface low pressure will traverse the waters on Friday, brining another round of gusty south winds, but uncertainty in this potential feature is high.

Improving marine conditions are then expected on Saturday during a break in the active weather. The progressive pattern is likely to bring further weather systems into the region from Sunday into early next week. -36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect through Thursday as the combination of King Tides, elevated seas, and the arrival of fresh swells likely lead to tidal overflow - impacts are most likely at high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. There is also a continued moderate to high sneaker wave threat through Thursday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
